newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Polifarbs may need foreign partner - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Polish Polifarbs may need foreign partner - analyst.

text.p: The planned merger of Polish paintmakers Polifarb Wroclaw and Polifarb Cieszyn may not be enough to defend their market share and they may still need a foreign partner, IB Austria said.
The merger plan, announced in December and expected to be completed by July 1997, has yet to win approval of Poland's Anti-Monopoly Office.

IB Austria analyst Remigiusz Tarka told a news conference on Tuesday that despite the new firm's likely growing profit margins it would still need a strategic foreign investor to defend its position on the market over the next several years.
"In future one can expect the new Polifarb to become a subject of interest of one of the major firms....at the turn of the century there could to be another big takeover," he said.
"The effect of (the domestic) merger is likely to last for only...two or three years," he added.

Tarka said the merged Polifarbs would likely control more than 40 percent of the Polish paints market but the market's growth and heating up competition from world leaders might force the new firm seek strategic partners to defend their market position.

Tarka said the use of paints per capita in Poland was only half of the European average of 14 kilograms but it was likely to grow at an annual rate of seven percent making Poland the most prospective market in Europe.
Tarka said that by joining forces the two companies would likely significantly improve profit margins due to lower costs and improved logistics.

IB Austria said the new firm could reach a net profit of 48 million zlotys this year, 65 million next year and 82 million in 1999 on sales of 616 million, 710 million and 805 million zlotys respectively.
Cieszyn had a 1996 net profit on 19.1 million zlotys on sales of 306.5 million and Wroclaw had a net of 18.6 million on 204.9-million-zloty-sales.

Tarka said shares of the Polifarbs were currently trading at a premium of 29 percent as investors were paying for future profits, but starting from next year they were likely to be trading at a discount, which Tarka saw at six percent in 1998.
IB Austria expected the firm's P/E ratio to fall below 10.6 in 1998 and 8.4 in 1999 from 18.3 in 1996 and expected 14.2 this year. -- Malgorzata Rzepka +48 22 653 9700
